first-principles-vs-analogy.core: Copy proven solutions when your context matches and stakes are low (analogy). Derive from bedrock facts when the problem is new, the stakes are high or your context differs (first principles). Know which mode you're in.

first_principles.problem: Engineers make architecture decisions that outlive the tools behind them. Most decisions are made by copying famous companies, which works until their hidden context doesn't match yours, and then you inherit their costs without their benefits.
truths: Tools change; constraints like physics, maths, budget and team size don't lie.
Copying is fast but assumes matching context.
derivation: Name the two modes: **analogy** (copy) and **first principles** (derive).
Watch for **cargo cults**: copying form without function.
Use the **algorithm**: assumptions → truths → rebuild → validate.
Pick the mode by **stakes, novelty and reversibility**.

analogy.title: The cook and the chef
analogy.story: The cook follows recipes and is efficient on routine nights. The chef understands what each ingredient does and can invent a dish when the pantry, altitude or guests change. A good kitchen needs both modes at the right time.
analogy.breaks: Kitchens have stable chemistry. Engineering constraints evolve with scale, so a first-principles answer must be re-derived as facts change.

example.title: Microservices for a 4-person startup
example.scenario: The CTO proposes microservices because Netflix uses them.

steps.label: Analogy check
steps.detail: Netflix has thousands of engineers needing independent deploys; this team has four.

steps.label: Truths
steps.detail: Each service adds deploys, monitoring and on-call that 4 people must run.

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: A well-structured monolith now, with clear module boundaries to split later.

example.outcome: the architecture fits today's facts, and the reasoning is written down so it can be revisited.

points: Copy form only if you also copy function.
Use the four-step algorithm for high-stakes calls.

check.q: When is reasoning by analogy the right choice?
check.a: For common, low-stakes, reversible decisions where your context matches the reference case.

check.q: What's cargo cult engineering?
check.a: Copying the visible form of a practice without the mechanism that made it work.

pattern-matching-vs-causal-reasoning.core: Pattern matching ("this looks like last time") is fast but follows correlation. Causal reasoning traces the mechanism that produced the symptom. Use fast instincts to mitigate and slow reasoning to find and design out root causes.

first_principles.problem: Incidents reward whoever speaks first, and the first explanation is usually a pattern match: the last deploy, last week's bug, two graphs moving together. Acting on correlation wastes time and leaves real causes in place.
truths: Correlation is everywhere in large metric sets.
Causes act through mechanisms you can describe and test.
Systems, not individuals, decide whether mistakes become outages.
derivation: Run **evidence-based Five Whys** ending in system fixes.
Use the causal chain to **design out failures** (timeouts, bulkheads, breakers).

analogy.title: A doctor diagnosing
analogy.story: A good doctor notices patterns ("flu season") but orders tests before prescribing, and then advises how to avoid the illness next time.
analogy.breaks: Patients describe symptoms. Systems only show metrics, so instrumentation decides how well you can reason.

example.title: An afternoon outage
example.scenario: DB CPU spikes right after a frontend deploy.

steps.label: Mitigate
steps.detail: Pause the backup job: the symptom clears.

steps.label: Cause
steps.detail: The table outgrew what the 3:00 backup could handle.

steps.label: Prevent
steps.detail: Add a scheduled-jobs view to the incident dashboard.

example.outcome: the real cause is fixed and the next responder sees scheduled jobs immediately.

check.q: What's the difference between correlation and causation?
check.a: Correlation means two things move together. Causation means one produces the other through a mechanism you can describe and test.

reversible-vs-irreversible-decisions.core: Classify decisions by the cost of reversing them. Move fast on two-way doors (Type 2), slow down on one-way doors (Type 1), and engineer escape hatches to turn the second into the first.

first_principles.problem: Organisations either debate everything (paralysis) or rush everything (lock-in). Both come from treating all decisions alike.
truths: Most decisions are cheap to reverse.
A few shape the system for years.
derivation: Assess on a **spectrum**: mechanism, time, impact, compounding.
**Convert** Type 1 to Type 2 with flags, abstractions, increments, pilots.
Set **approval thresholds** proportional to reversal cost.

analogy.title: Doors in a house
analogy.story: Most doors swing both ways and you walk through without thinking. A few lock behind you, and those you check carefully. And sometimes you can install a handle on the other side.
analogy.breaks: Doors are visibly different. Decision reversibility has to be assessed, and it changes over time.

example.title: A quarter of decisions
example.scenario: A platform team reviews how it made 40 decisions.

steps.label: Audit
steps.detail: Most delays came from cheap, reversible choices.

steps.label: Change
steps.detail: Introduce tiers and decision deadlines.

example.outcome: velocity rises without increasing risk.

check.q: Which type of decision deserves an RFC?
check.a: Type 1 decisions with high impact and expensive reversal.

check.q: How can you make a Type 1 decision more reversible?
check.a: Feature flags, abstraction layers, incremental migration or pilots.

adrs-and-rfcs.core: Write down why, not just what. RFCs gather input before a significant decision; ADRs record each decision's context and consequences immutably, next to the code, so future engineers understand and can safely change it.

first_principles.problem: Organisations forget why systems are built the way they are. New engineers either fear changing anything or repeat old mistakes, and big decisions get made without input from the teams they affect.
derivation: Use **RFCs** before big, shared, irreversible decisions.
Record every significant decision in a short, immutable **ADR**.
Make it stick with **PR gates** and **tooling**.

analogy.title: Planning permission and the deeds
analogy.story: You apply for planning permission (RFC) before building, gathering comments. Once built, the deeds and notes (ADRs) record what was decided and why, for every future owner.
analogy.breaks: Property records are legally required. Decision records survive only if the team makes them part of the workflow.

example.title: A database migration end to end
example.scenario: The order service's database keeps failing.

steps.label: RFC
steps.detail: Problem data, options, risks.

steps.label: ADR
steps.detail: Records the decision and costs.

steps.label: Years later
steps.detail: A new engineer reads 0007 before proposing a change.

example.outcome: decisions get better input up front and stay understandable for years.

check.q: What three sections form the core of an ADR?
check.a: Context, Decision and Consequences.

the-iron-triangle.core: Velocity, reliability and cost compete for the same finite resources. Pick the two your business phase needs, measure all three, sacrifice the third on purpose, and use error budgets as the release valve.

first_principles.problem: Organisations want everything at once and end up sacrificing reliability silently, until outages and burnout force a reckoning.
derivation: Define each vertex with **metrics** (DORA, SLOs, full cost).
Choose by **business phase** and write it down.
Spot the triangle in **daily platform choices**.

analogy.title: Fast, good, cheap
analogy.story: The old contractor's sign: pick any two. Good contractors tell you which two you're getting before they start.
analogy.breaks: A contractor's job ends; a system keeps running, so the sacrificed side keeps costing.

example.title: A scale-up's yearly plan
example.scenario: Leadership plans next year's engineering priorities.

steps.label: Explicit
steps.detail: Cost will rise 30% for multi-AZ and SRE hires.

steps.label: Guard
steps.detail: An error budget policy decides freezes.

example.outcome: everyone knows what's being traded and why.

check.q: What does the Iron Triangle say you can't do?
check.a: Maximise velocity, reliability and cost efficiency simultaneously.

tradeoff-analysis.core: Every engineering choice gains something and gives something up. Name the axes, weigh options against your real constraints (including reversibility), choose deliberately, and record the reasoning.

first_principles.problem: Teams look for 'the right answer', copy popular choices, or decide by gut, then can't explain or revisit the decision later.
truths: True trade-offs worsen one quality to improve another.
Context decides which downsides are tolerable.
Reversibility changes how careful you must be.
derivation: Name recurring **axes**: simplicity/flexibility, build/buy, lock-in, speed/safety.
Use the **five-step framework** and record an ADR.

analogy.title: Buying the right car for your life
analogy.story: There's no best car. A family of five and a city commuter choose differently, and both are right.
analogy.breaks: Cars are easy to compare on paper. Software costs often appear later, so seek real experience reports.

example.title: Picking an auth solution

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.detail: Build fails on TCO and security risk.

steps.label: Record
steps.detail: Revisit if pricing exceeds threshold.

example.outcome: a clear, recorded choice that can be challenged with data later.

check.q: What makes something a true trade-off?
check.a: Improving one quality necessarily degrades another.

risk-modeling.core: Risk = likelihood × impact. Write risks down, score them consistently, put a price on them, choose a deliberate response, find silent failures with FMEA, and build general resilience for what you can't predict.

first_principles.problem: Engineering decisions are bets, but most teams never name them. Risks live in people's heads, priorities follow fear rather than exposure, and silent failures surprise everyone.
derivation: Use **FMEA** for detection gaps; build **resilience** for black swans.

analogy.title: Running a household
analogy.story: You insure the house, fix the leaking roof first, list what needs maintenance, and keep an emergency fund for what you can't foresee.
analogy.breaks: Households have decades of shared wisdom. Systems need their own analysis.

example.title: A platform team's first risk review

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Untested backups and silent cron failures move to the top.

steps.label: Action
steps.detail: Owners and dates; reviewed quarterly.

example.outcome: risk becomes a managed portfolio instead of a source of surprises.

check.q: What are the four risk responses?
check.a: Avoid, mitigate, transfer and accept.

strangler-fig-migration.core: Don't rewrite legacy systems in one big bang. Put a proxy in front, replace one slice at a time, sync data carefully (shared DB, dual writes, CDC), shift traffic gradually, and actually delete the old code.

first_principles.problem: Legacy monoliths are scary to change and tempting to rewrite. Big-bang rewrites freeze the business, chase a moving target and miss hidden rules.
truths: Data is shared and hard to split.

analogy.title: The strangler fig
analogy.story: A fig grows around a host tree, slowly taking over until the host is gone and the fig stands alone.
analogy.breaks: Figs need no budget. Migrations need sustained funding and clear completion goals.

example.title: Migrating a billing monolith

steps.label: Progress
steps.detail: Tracked by % of endpoints migrated each quarter.

example.outcome: the legacy system is replaced without a single big-risk cutover.

check.q: What are the three phases?
check.a: Intercept, replace, and eliminate.

systems-thinking-dynamics.core: Complex systems behave through stocks, flows, delays and feedback loops. See behaviours over time, recognise loops and archetypes, beware gamed metrics, and intervene at high-leverage points.

first_principles.problem: Linear thinking fixes events and misses the loops that recreate them. Incentives backfire, autoscalers oscillate and problems snowball.

analogy.title: A bathtub with a thermostat and a slow tap
analogy.story: The water level depends on tap and drain rates, adjusts toward a target, lags behind your actions, and can overflow if you keep turning the tap.
analogy.breaks: Bathtubs are simple. Real systems have many interlocking loops, so mapping them takes effort.

example.title: On-call burnout

steps.label: Intervention
steps.detail: Each alert must have an owner and an SLO link, which cut noise by half.

example.outcome: the system's structure changes, so the behaviour changes.

check.q: What's a stock and a flow?
check.a: A stock is an accumulation (like backlog); flows are the rates that increase or decrease it.

complexity-frameworks.core: Problems differ in how knowable their cause and effect are. Cynefin sorts them into Clear, Complicated, Complex and Chaotic, each with its own approach, and warns that complacent 'clear' systems can collapse into chaos.

first_principles.problem: Using one problem-solving style everywhere fails: best practices break in complex situations, analysis stalls during chaos, and 'solved' systems fail suddenly.
truths: Ordered systems are analysable; unordered ones emerge.
Each domain needs a different action order.
derivation: Watch the **cliff** from Clear to Chaotic.
Apply it to **incidents and platform design**.

analogy.title: A kitchen through the day
analogy.story: Boiling eggs (clear), baking a wedding cake (complicated), inventing a dish (complex), and a grease fire (chaotic) each need a different approach.
analogy.breaks: Kitchens are small. Systems can be in several domains at once, so classify parts separately.

example.title: A platform team's week
example.scenario: Routine tickets, a performance mystery, and a sudden outage.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Each piece of work gets the right method.

example.outcome: less wasted effort and faster recovery.

check.q: What is the action order in the complex domain?
check.a: Probe, sense, respond: run safe experiments and learn from what emerges.

cognitive-biases.core: Mental shortcuts cause predictable errors: normalising warnings, confirming favourite theories, honouring sunk costs, judging with hindsight, learning only from survivors and anchoring on first numbers. Counter them with process, not willpower.

first_principles.problem: Engineers make systematic mistakes in incidents, estimates, project decisions and post-mortems because these biases operate automatically under pressure.
derivation: **Normalisation of deviance** → actionable alerts, review what's ignored.
**Sunk cost** → decide on future value, kill criteria.

analogy.title: Pilots' checklists
analogy.story: Pilots are highly skilled, yet they use checklists because skill doesn't prevent predictable lapses under stress.
analogy.breaks: Aviation checklists are mature. Engineering teams must build their own.

example.title: An incident review

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Alert curation and hypothesis time-boxing added to incident practice.

example.outcome: the team makes fewer predictable mistakes.

check.q: Why are checklists effective against bias?
check.a: They force deliberate steps that automatic shortcuts would skip.

economic-engineering.core: Engineers spend company money with every decision. Count total cost of ownership, understand CAPEX vs OPEX, include opportunity and coordination costs, track unit economics and practise FinOps.

first_principles.problem: Engineering decisions are made on sticker price or excitement, hiding people costs, opportunity costs and coordination overhead.

analogy.title: Running a small business
analogy.story: You price products with all costs included, watch margin per sale, and know hiring more staff doesn't always increase output.
analogy.breaks: Small businesses see money directly. Engineering costs hide in salaries and cloud bills.

example.title: Build vs buy observability
example.scenario: Self-host Prometheus stack or buy SaaS?

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: SaaS chosen on TCO; unit cost reviewed quarterly.

example.outcome: engineering choices are made like business investments.

check.q: What does TCO capture that sticker price doesn't?
check.a: Ongoing operation, people time, training, downtime and exit costs.

bugs-and-anomalies.core: Name the kind of bug before hunting it: Bohrbugs reproduce, Heisenbugs hide when observed, Mandelbugs emerge from complexity, Schroedinbugs were always broken, rot comes from a changing environment, and distributed systems add their own anomalies.

first_principles.problem: Using one debugging approach for every failure wastes hours: breakpoints hide races, single-variable tests miss interactions, and nobody suspects that unchanged code rotted.
truths: Bug types respond to different tools.

analogy.title: A doctor's differential diagnosis
analogy.story: Symptoms suggest a category, the category suggests tests, and tests confirm before treatment.
analogy.breaks: Medicine has extensive references. Engineering teams build their own playbooks per bug type.

example.title: Triage of three bugs
example.scenario: A wrong total, a rare crash and an old script failure.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: All three fixed in a day with the right tools.

example.outcome: diagnosis first makes debugging fast.

check.q: What's a Heisenbug?
check.a: A bug that disappears or changes when you try to observe it.

strategic-visualization.core: Make strategy visible. Wardley maps place components by user visibility and evolution to show where to build, buy or move next; SWOT summarises your capabilities and risks. Together they turn opinion debates into evidence-based choices.

first_principles.problem: High-stakes tech decisions are argued from preference. Without a shared view of the landscape, teams build commodities, ignore evolution and repeat circular debates.
truths: Capabilities determine which moves are realistic.

analogy.title: Planning a journey
analogy.story: A map shows the terrain and roads under construction; knowing your car and budget tells you which route to take.
analogy.breaks: Roads change slowly. Tech landscapes shift within months.

example.title: Deciding the CI/CD strategy
example.scenario: Build a custom pipeline or adopt a product?

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: The debate ends in 30 minutes with a clear rationale.

example.outcome: the team invests only where it differentiates.

check.q: What do the two Wardley axes represent?
check.a: Visibility to the user (value chain) and evolution (genesis to commodity).

project-management-fundamentals.core: Project management is choosing what to build, in what order, and getting it done. Know why waterfall exists, use Agile values with Scrum or Kanban as the work demands, estimate honestly, clarify PM vs EM roles, structure tickets, and run meetings that earn their cost.

first_principles.problem: Teams either drown in process or reject it entirely, estimate poorly, blur roles and burn time in purposeless meetings.
derivation: Pick **Scrum or Kanban** by work type.

analogy.title: Running a kitchen
analogy.story: You plan the menu (PM), run the kitchen (EM), cook in courses or à la carte (Scrum/Kanban), estimate prep times from experience, and keep briefings short.
analogy.breaks: Kitchens have stable recipes. Software work is more uncertain, so iterate.

example.title: A new team sets up its process

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Lightweight process tuned to the team's work.

example.outcome: process supports delivery instead of replacing it.

check.q: What's the difference between Agile and Scrum?
check.a: Agile is a set of values; Scrum is one specific framework for applying them.

strategic-planning.core: Strategy aligns effort. Use KPIs to watch health, OKRs to drive deliberate change, choose wartime or peacetime leadership by situation, run a quarterly plan–execute–review cycle, and trace every ticket to a goal.

first_principles.problem: Growing organisations lose shared direction; teams work hard on conflicting things, and strategy never reaches daily work.
truths: Health and change need different tools.

analogy.title: Steering a ship
analogy.story: Instruments show the ship is healthy (KPIs), the destination sets the course (OKRs), the captain changes style in storms, and every crew member knows their part.
analogy.breaks: Ships have one captain. Organisations need alignment across many leaders.

example.title: A platform team's quarter
example.scenario: From company goal to daily work.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Everyone can explain how their work moves a KR.

example.outcome: effort compounds toward shared goals.

check.q: What is a Key Result?
check.a: A measurable outcome showing progress toward an objective.

technical-due-diligence.core: Technical due diligence inspects everything you're about to buy: people, architecture, code, security and operations. Find the tech debt bombs, plan an integration that avoids the rewrite trap, and report risks in business terms.

first_principles.problem: Acquirers pay for products and inherit hidden liabilities and integration failures that destroy the value they bought.
derivation: Run a structured **process** with a data room.

analogy.title: Buying a house properly
analogy.story: Survey before you buy, price in the repairs, and don't knock down the parts that make it valuable after moving in.
analogy.breaks: Houses don't have employees who might leave. Acquisitions do.

example.title: A $50M acquisition

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Fair price, retention terms and a 90-day remediation plan.

example.outcome: the deal reflects technical reality.

check.q: What are the five pillars of a tech stack audit?
check.a: People, architecture, code, security, and operations/cost.

ethical-engineering.core: Code enforces rules on people at scale, so engineers share responsibility for its effects. Build privacy in, refuse dark patterns, make software accessible, check automated decisions for bias, and embed ethics in process.

first_principles.problem: Ethics is treated as legal's job, yet engineers implement the data flows, defaults and interfaces that help or harm users.

analogy.title: Architecture and building codes
analogy.story: Architects design for safety, accessibility and privacy from the start, guided by codes and reviews.
analogy.breaks: Buildings are inspected. Software ethics relies more on internal practice.

example.title: Launching a sign-up flow

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Users trust the product and it meets regulations.

example.outcome: products respect users by design.

check.q: What does Privacy by Design require?
check.a: Building data protection into the system's architecture from the start, not adding it later.

innovation-tokens.core: Teams can only absorb a few unproven technologies (~3 innovation tokens). Use boring, proven tech by default, count novelty's hidden costs, and spend tokens only on core problems where they buy real advantage.

first_principles.problem: Engineers adopt shiny new tools everywhere and end up operating a stack full of unknown failure modes, with no capacity left for what differentiates the business.
truths: Proven tech has known failure modes.
derivation: Spend only on **core, unsolved, high-value** problems.

analogy.title: A small budget for risky bets
analogy.story: With only three risky bets to make, you'd place them where the payoff matters most and play everything else safe.
analogy.breaks: Bets resolve once. Technologies keep costing until they become boring or are removed.

example.title: A new product's stack

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: One token on the core engine; everything else proven.

example.outcome: the team innovates where it counts and sleeps at night.

check.q: Who coined 'innovation tokens'?
check.a: Dan McKinley, in 'Choose Boring Technology'.

consensus-building.core: Fast decisions with real buy-in come from a lifecycle: prepare with one-on-one conversations (Nemawashi), decide with clear roles and alternatives (SPADE), then execute together (disagree and commit).

first_principles.problem: Teams either decide autocratically and get resistance, or seek unanimous agreement and stall for weeks.

analogy.title: Planning a group trip
analogy.story: Talk to everyone about preferences first, agree who books and by when, then everyone goes along cheerfully.
analogy.breaks: Trips are low stakes. Engineering decisions affect livelihoods, so fairness of process matters more.

example.title: Choosing an observability vendor

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Decision in two weeks instead of two months.

example.outcome: decisions are fast and stick.

check.q: Why combine Nemawashi and SPADE?
check.a: Nemawashi builds alignment beforehand; SPADE ensures someone clearly decides.

technological-entropy.core: Software decays by default: dependencies drift, designs erode, knowledge leaks and data goes stale. Fight entropy continuously: fix broken windows quickly, leave code cleaner, refactor as hygiene and automate decay detection.

first_principles.problem: Teams treat working code as finished, then face expensive emergency upgrades and rewrites when decay finally hurts.
truths: Disorder is free; order costs energy.

analogy.title: Maintaining a garden
analogy.story: Weeds grow without help. A little weeding every week keeps the garden healthy; neglect for a year means starting over.
analogy.breaks: Gardens show weeds visibly. Software decay is often invisible without metrics.

example.title: A healthy codebase policy

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: The codebase gets healthier each quarter.

example.outcome: entropy is held back continuously instead of by crisis.

check.q: Name the four modes of software rot.
check.a: Dependency rot, design rot, knowledge rot and data rot.
